# Abstract

## Ecological Scope and Headline Trajectory

The Canadian Prairies (`1,07M km²`, `21.191` active 5-arcminute cells) form the northernmost grassland and aspen-parkland extension of the Great Plains bison-hunting economy. Glacial retreat and draining of Lake Agassiz opened the plains progressively from west to east during the Early Holocene.

Reconstructed across four physiographic divisions under CENTAUR-II from `10000BC` to `1600AD`, regional population rises from `150` late-glacial foothill hunters in `10000BC` to `12,9k` in `5000BC` and `36,3k` at `0AD`. Communal buffalo jumps, timber pounds and Oxbow-Besant winter encampments multiplied steadily across the Saskatchewan and Red-Assiniboine drainages [@brink2008; @peck2011; @dyck1970oxbow].

Aggregate population reaches a late pre-contact plateau of `46k` across `1500AD` and `1550AD` (`4,29` persons per `100 km²`), easing marginally by `1,52%` to `45,3k` by `1600AD`.

## Sub-Regional Contrasts and Composite Integration

Peak sub-regional density concentrates in the Rocky Mountain Foothills and Bow-Oldman Plains (`9,18` persons per `100 km²`, `27,2%` of regional population). Meanwhile, the expansive Aspen Parkland and North Saskatchewan Valley holds the largest total demographic share (`29,3%`, `13,5k`).

Spatial allocation links `66` catalogued aggregation hubs (`67` ledger candidates with `1` duplicate-alias consolidation) to a multi-registry North American radiocarbon composite (`93.358` unique site-periods across `4.457` domestic catchments, `14,12x` baseline density). Fitted via non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging ($\tau_1 = 1,41$, raw nugget `0,000`, regularised nugget-to-sill `0,04`, $R^2 = 0,999$), the grid maintains continuous density gradients into Montana, North Dakota and Minnesota across the forty-ninth parallel.

# Background

## Grassland Ecology and Historiographic Context

### Beyond Uniform Steppe Abstractions

Earlier macro-scale continental atlases treated the Canadian Prairies as uniform low-density steppe, overlooking sharp ecological contrasts among chinook-warmed foothill wintering coulees, semi-arid Palliser mixedgrass plains and fertile Red River horticultural floodplains [@bamforth1988; @boyd2006; @peck2011].

In practice, bison herd seasonality imposed a strict spatial rhythm on human aggregation across the northern plains. Winter survival favoured sheltered aspen-grove coulees, riverine gallery forests and foothills topography where timber fuel, flowing water and reliable wind-driven snow-free grazing coincided [@brink2008; @walker1992; @frison2004].

### Division Design and Benchmark Series

CENTAUR-II divides `1.071.166 km²` into four physiographically coherent sub-regions aligned to precipitation belts, grassland biomes and major drainage basins (Table \ref{tab:subregions}). Each sub-region carries a `23`-benchmark series spanning `10000BC` to `1600AD`.

## Four Physiographic Divisions

### Rocky Mountain Foothills and Bow-Oldman Plains

The Rocky Mountain Foothills and Bow-Oldman Plains (`136.211 km²`, `12,7%` of module area) trace the sheltered fescue-grassland wintering belt along the Porcupine Hills, Bow, Oldman and Milk rivers [@brink2008; @forbis1977].

Warm winter chinook winds periodically stripped snowpack from rolling fescue benches, making the Porcupine Hills and Oldman valley an ideal cold-season wintering zone. This foothill belt formed the ancestral heartland of Niitsitapi (`Blackfoot`) communal bison-drive complexes including Head-Smashed-In, Old Women's Buffalo Jump and Writing-On-Stone [@brink2008; @mckinnon1986paleoenvironments].

### Aspen Parkland and North Saskatchewan Valley

Across the northern forest-grassland ecotone, the Aspen Parkland and North Saskatchewan Valley (`456.477 km²`, `42,6%`) spans wooded parkland coulees and broad valley terraces from the upper Saskatchewan forks toward central Alberta [@walker1992; @peck2011].

Aspen bluffs sheltered wintering bison herds against Arctic cold fronts while providing predictable firewood, berry harvests and sheltered winter tipi clearings. Oxbow, Besant and Plains Cree communities clustered seasonally around Wanuskewin, Bushfield West, Below Forks and Bodo [@walker1992; @roskowski2004geoarchaeology].

### South Saskatchewan Mixedgrass Steppe and Qu'Appelle

Southward, the South Saskatchewan Mixedgrass Steppe and Qu'Appelle (`217.723 km²`, `20,3%`) encompasses drier Palliser grasslands and deeply incised glacial spillways stretching across southern Saskatchewan [@walde2006; @vickers1994].

Lower annual precipitation and scarcer upland timber restricted sedentary residence to river valley gallery woods and spring-fed coulees. Even under dry steppe regimes, Avonlea and Mortlach bow-and-arrow hunters operated highly productive communal pounds at Gull Lake, Avonlea and Mortlach [@walde2006; @kobes2019river].

### Red-Assiniboine Plains and Lake Manitoba Lowlands

Eastward, the Red-Assiniboine Plains and Lake Manitoba Lowlands (`260.755 km²`, `24,3%`) join glacial Lake Agassiz clay plains with productive marshlands, oak savannas and tallgrass floodplains [@boyd2006; @peck2011].

Laurel and Blackduck woodland communities paired prairie-margin bison drives with lake-edge fisheries and northern wild-rice wetlands. By late precontact centuries, village farmers at Lockport added storage-pit maize horticulture along rich Red River alluvial levees alongside ceremonial centres at Lowton and Stott [@boyd2006; @peck2011].

# Methodology

## Benchmark Cadence and Bison-Pound Demographic Anchors

Each sub-regional series spans `23` chronological anchors from `10000BC` to `1600AD`. Benchmarks advance in millennial steps before `0AD`, bicentennial steps through `1000AD`, centennial steps through `1500AD` and fifty-year resolution at `1550AD` and `1600AD`.

Regional population totals synthesise communal kill-site processing labour requirements [@brink2008; @frison2004], winter campsite hearth counts [@dyck1970oxbow; @walker1992], northern plains radiocarbon probability distributions [@kelly2025; @peck2011] and ethnohistoric contact estimates [@ubelaker2006].

Communal bison procurement demanded strict seasonal coordination between winter coulee aggregations and warm-season dispersed foraging circuits [@brink2008; @frison2004]. Each sub-regional series carries symmetric `+/- 8%` uncertainty intervals anchored to ethnographic band-size dispersion [@ubelaker2006].

## Multi-Registry Radiocarbon Composite and Matérn Kriging

Rural demographic allocation across the `21.191` active cells of the Canadian Prairies draws on the continental North American radiocarbon composite (`481.752` terrestrial 5-arcminute cells). This surface combines global syntheses (`c14bazAAR` and `p3k14c`) [@bird2022p3k14c] with the Canadian Archaeological Radiocarbon Database (`CARD`), provincial heritage inventories in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, United States state archaeological site files, Greenland *Nunniffiit* registers and regional cultural resource management surveys.

After spatial and temporal deduplication by catchment and 200-year bin, the composite contains `93.358` unique site-periods across `4.457` domestic Voronoi catchments (`2.678` active inhabited catchments, `60,09%` coverage). That footprint reaches `14,12x` baseline observation density above `c14bazAAR` alone, with a median catchment Voronoi radius of `27,36 km` and a 90th-percentile radius of `59,92 km`.

To prevent artificial border cliffs across the forty-ninth parallel into Montana, North Dakota and Minnesota, `171` cross-frontier buffer catchments condition density gradients up to `300 km` beyond the national boundary. Weighted least-squares covariates incorporating coastal proximity, `13,5 km` fluvial distance decay, terrain slope and ecological potential feed 2D Paciorek-Schervish non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging across `10` Holocene horizons anchored to Kelly et al. [@kelly2025] regional curves.

## Settlement Subtraction and Border Feathering

From primary Plains monographs and provincial heritage files, `66` persistent bison-jump, winter-village, horticultural and ceremonial aggregation hubs are geolocated with bounded demographic trajectories. Nearby camp clusters at major kill canyons are consolidated in the source ledger so composite landforms are not double-counted.

At every benchmark year, active settlement populations are subtracted from their enclosing sub-region before distributing remaining rural band populations proportional to the kriged surface inside the areal mask and applying two passes of a 4-pixel separable border smoother.

# Testing and Validation

Three quantitative checks govern the Canadian Prairies module prior to compilation:

1. **Variogram Sharpness and Fit**: Across all `10` Holocene horizons of the North American Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) surface, dimensionless range holds at $\tau_1 = 1,41$ (`1,4144 <= 1,80`) and $\tau_2 = 2,62$ (`2,6166`), with raw nugget-to-sill equal to `0,000` (`0,04` regularised, below the `0,45` ceiling). Weighted least-squares covariates remain active on every horizon, achieving $R^2 = 0,999$ (`0,9991` to `0,9993`), reported in Table \ref{tab:kriging}.
2. **Gazetteer and Ledger Reconciliation**: Cross-checking `66` included aggregation hubs against `67` source-ledger candidates yields `1` documented duplicate-alias consolidation (`Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump` merged within `2 km` into the canonical site entry), `0` unaccounted records and `0` schema faults. Sub-regional coverage spans `23` sites in Foothills-Bow, `13` in Aspen Parkland, `17` in South Saskatchewan-Palliser and `13` in Red-Assiniboine.
3. **Cross-Frontier Seam Continuity**: Inter-regional borders with Northern Cascadia and Alaska, Northern Canada and Greenland, Hudson Bay and the Extreme Northern Plains and Souris-Red-Rainy basins of the United States exhibit continuous density transitions without step-function jumps.

# Results

## Glacial Lake Retreat and Early Bison Hunters (10000BC to 6000BC)

### Ice-Free Foothills and Proglacial Lake Barriers

In `10000BC`, glacial Lake Agassiz and the retreating Laurentide ice margin confined human occupation to the ice-free western foothills (`150` inhabitants, `138` to `162`). The Saskatchewan and Red River plains remained inundated or ice-covered and therefore held zero inhabitants.

Rapid deglaciation and catastrophic draining of glacial lake basins between `9000BC` (`800`) and `7000BC` (`5,2k`) opened the interior plains from west to east. Palaeoindian Agate Basin, Scottsbluff and Cody Complex bison hunters rapidly colonised the Aspen Parkland (`1,5k` in `7000BC`), Palliser steppe (`1,1k`) and Red-Assiniboine lowlands (`1k`) [@walker1992; @peck2011].

### Early Gazetteer Footholds and West-to-East Colonisation

Early post-glacial sites documented in the gazetteer capture this chronological gradient cleanly. In the western foothills and northwestern parkland corridor, occupation began at Vermilion Lakes (`85` peak, occupied from `8800BC`) and Fletcher (`75`, `7800BC`), complemented by Charlie Lake Cave bison assemblages [@vallieres2004paleoindian].

Farther east, Heron Eden (`75`, `7900BC`) and Niska (`75`, `7200BC`) mark early Saskatchewan occupancy alongside Saskatoon Mountain (`95`, `7400BC`) and St. Louis (`70`, `7200BC`) in central parkland, while Sinnock (`65`, `7200BC`) traces pioneer settlement along the draining Lake Agassiz margin. By `6000BC`, total prairie population reached `8,8k` across all four divisions.

## Altithermal Parkland Shift and Middle Holocene Jump Complexes (5000BC to 1000BC)

### Warm-Dry Grassland Contraction and River-Bend Refugia

During the mid-Holocene Altithermal warm-dry phase (`5500BC` to `3000BC`), drier grassland conditions pushed bison herds and human winter camps toward the Aspen Parkland, foothill coulees and sheltered river bends [@walker1992; @dyck1970oxbow]. Despite arid steppe stress, better-watered ecotone valleys supported steady growth from `12,9k` in `5000BC` to `22,3k` in `3000BC` and `32k` in `1000BC`.

Geoarchaeological and palaeobotanical investigations along the Saskatchewan forks, Cold Lake and Head-Smashed-In document shifting river floodplains, carbon-isotope grassland composition changes and multi-component camp stratification across this interval [@roskowski2004geoarchaeology; @jass2017underwater; @mckinnon1986paleoenvironments].

### Emergence of Monumental Jumps and Ceremonial Circles

Major aggregation hubs crystalised during this epoch where topographical traps met reliable timber and winter water. Wanuskewin (`4000BC` onward, reaching `450` peak) and Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump (`3500BC` onward, reaching `650` peak) anchored multi-millennial gathering circuits, alongside Gowen (`95`, `4300BC` to `3200BC`), Below Forks (`110`, `4200BC` to `1600BC`), Majorville Medicine Wheel (`290`, `2500BC` onward) and Tailrace Bay (`280`, `2000BC` onward) [@brink2008; @walker1992; @roskowski2004geoarchaeology].

By `1000BC`, Pelican Lake, Oxbow and McKean-Hanna populations had established dense winter residence patterns across all four basins. Aspen Parkland led with `9,3k` inhabitants, followed by Foothills-Bow (`8,4k`), Red-Assiniboine (`7,9k`) and South Saskatchewan-Palliser (`6,4k`) [@peck2011; @dyck1970oxbow].

## Bow-and-Arrow Pounds, Plains Villages and Maize Outliers (0AD to 1500AD)

At `0AD`, Canadian Prairie population reached `36,3k` (`33,4k` to `39,2k`), growing steadily to `43,5k` in `800AD`, `44,5k` in `1000AD` and `46k` by `1500AD` (Figure \ref{fig:traj}). Adoption of the bow and arrow alongside Besant and Avonlea pottery (`200AD` to `800AD`) raised communal hunting efficiency across open grasslands through constructed timber-corral pounds and cliff drives [@vickers1994; @walde2006; @tischer2000egpn].

### Rocky Mountain Foothills and Bow-Oldman Plains

Along the foothill wintering belt, Head-Smashed-In (`650` peak in `1500AD`) operated alongside Old Women's Buffalo Jump (`460` peak), Writing-On-Stone (`410`), Saamis (`320`), Ross (`280`), Castle Forks (`250`) and Morkin (`240`). Numerous specialised kill-and-processing stations such as EgPn-440, Fish Creek and Happy Valley bridged surrounding coulees [@brink2008; @tischer2000egpn; @wickham2005efpm; @shortt1993happy].

Foothill population rose from `9,6k` at `0AD` to `12,5k` in `1500AD`, sustaining the highest prairie density at `9,18` persons per `100 km²`. Later fourteenth-to-sixteenth-century fortified earthwork occupation at Cluny Fortified Village (`250` peak) attests to Middle Missouri-style village experimentation on the Bow River [@forbis1977; @walde2006].

### Aspen Parkland and South Saskatchewan Steppe

Across the North Saskatchewan and parkland belt, Wanuskewin (`450` peak, incorporating multi-component sites such as Red Tail and Newo Asiniak), Bushfield West (`440`), Bodo Archaeological Site (`410`), Francois-Finlay (`340`), Goldsworthy (`250`) and Tschetter (`240`) supported an expansion from `10,6k` at `0AD` to `13,5k` by `1500AD` [@kelly1986newo; @williams2015archaeological; @peck2011].

In the drier South Saskatchewan and Qu'Appelle valleys, Avonlea and Mortlach communal hunting systems at Gull Lake (`420`), Avonlea (`390`), Mortlach (`380`), Estuary Bison Pound (`270`), Bakken-Wright (`270`) and Melhagen (`260`) lifted population from `7,2k` at `0AD` to `9k` from `1200AD` to `1550AD` [@walde2006; @kobes2019river]. Despite open shortgrass terrain, coulee springs and gallery timber sustained predictable seasonal pounds.

### Red-Assiniboine Plains and Northern Maize Horticulture

In the Red-Assiniboine and Lake Manitoba lowlands, Laurel, Blackduck and Vickers Focus communities combined bison procurement with intensive marsh fisheries and northern maize horticulture [@boyd2006; @peck2011]. Storage-pit maize cultivation at Lockport (`680` peak overall, `480` in `1500AD`) marked the northernmost prehistoric farming outlier on the Canadian plains.

Alongside Lockport, lake-margin and parkland villages at Aschkibokahn (`390`), Lowton (`390`), Stott (`380`), Duck Bay (`340`), Jackson (`310`), Twin Fawns (`310`) and Whiteshell Petroforms (`310`) lifted eastern lowland population from `8,9k` at `0AD` to `11k` in `1400AD` to `1550AD` (`4,22` persons per `100 km²`). Figure \ref{fig:shares} charts the long-run compositional balance across all four sub-regions.

## Protohistoric Plateau and Early Contact Threshold (1500AD to 1600AD)

Prairie population stabilised on a plateau of `46k` across `1500AD` and `1550AD` (`4,29` persons per `100 km²`), held in equilibrium by foothill wintering capacity, parkland ecotone diversity and steppe bison carrying limits. Between `1550AD` and `1600AD`, regional totals dipped slightly by `1,52%` (`700` inhabitants) to `45,3k`.

That mild terminal contraction reflects Little Ice Age winter severity fluctuations and early protohistoric indirect epidemiological disruption ahead of eighteenth-century equestrian transformation [@ubelaker2006; @walde2006]. # Limitations

## Mobile Tipi-Ring Visibility and CRM Survey Bias

Three taphonomic and sampling constraints qualify the Canadian Prairies series. First, mobile equestrian-era precursor bands lived primarily in skin tipis that left shallow stone circles vulnerable to deflation and agricultural ploughing [@frison2004; @bird2022p3k14c].

By contrast, stratified buffalo-jump bonebeds and river-valley earthworks accumulate abundant datable charcoal and bone, biasing raw radiocarbon tallies toward cliff drives and village pits [@brink2008].

Second, heritage compliance surveys concentrate heavily along urban river corridors (`Calgary`, `Saskatoon`, `Qu'Appelle`, `Winnipeg`) and commercial forestry or petroleum leases in central and northern Alberta [@statz2020efficiency; @kobes2019river]. Vast stretches of interior mixedgrass prairie and boreal-margin muskeg remain far more sparsely tested.

## Alluvial Burial and Uncertainty Envelopes

Third, post-glacial spring flooding in the Red, Assiniboine and Saskatchewan valleys buries early Holocene campsites beneath thick alluvial silt [@roskowski2004geoarchaeology]. Across the drained Lake Agassiz floor, intensive modern cultivation also disturbs shallow Woodland horizons and small maize garden plots [@boyd2006].

Finally, the uniform `+/- 8%` uncertainty envelope captures macro-level benchmark carrying-capacity spread rather than statistical confidence intervals on bison-pound bone counts [@ubelaker2006; @peck2011].

Future subsurface geophysical survey along buried palaeochannels may raise early Holocene river-valley estimates slightly without altering the late pre-contact ceiling.

# Conclusion

## From Glacial Margin to Pre-Contact Equilibrium

The Canadian Prairies illustrate a long-run transition from `150` late-glacial foothill bison hunters in `10000BC` to a resilient nomadic and parkland society of `46k` inhabitants in `1500AD` to `1550AD` (`45,3k` in `1600AD`).

Once proglacial lakes drained, hunter-gatherer mobility filled the grasslands quickly, reaching nearly three-quarters of peak capacity by `1000BC` (`32k`).

Later adoption of the bow and arrow alongside timber bison pounds lifted carrying capacity to its mature pre-contact ceiling without exhausting winter forage refugia.

## Sub-Regional Asymmetry and Plains Diversity

Ecological contrast governed demographic geography throughout the Holocene across every precipitation belt.

Chinook-moderated foothill valleys sustained `9,18` persons per `100 km²`, more than double the mixedgrass Palliser steppe (`4,13`) and Red-Assiniboine lowlands (`4,22`). Across the broad northern ecotone, lower winter density across woodland-steppe margins kept Aspen Parkland mean density at `2,96` persons per `100 km²`.

At the eastern grassland edge, horticultural experimentation at Lockport (`680` peak overall, `480` in `1500AD`) demonstrates that storage-pit maize farming penetrated deep into northern river valleys before direct European contact [@boyd2006]. Simultaneously, fourteenth-to-sixteenth-century fortified plains earthworks at Cluny (`250` peak) show parallel village experimentation along the Bow River [@forbis1977].

## Composite Conditioning and Plains Continuity

Integrating `66` persistent aggregation centres (`67` ledger candidates) with multi-registry North American Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging calibrated across `93.358` unique site-periods resolves forty-ninth-parallel border cliffs into Montana and North Dakota.

Adjacent transitions toward the Rocky Mountain foothills, boreal Saskatchewan and northern Red River forests remain continuous across all `23` temporal benchmarks.

Taken together, the composite raster surface and reconciled gazetteer ground northern plains historical demography in documented archaeological site distributions without artificial border discontinuities.

Regional demographic reconstructions thus remain directly extensible southward into the Missouri and Mississippi basins as adjacent chapters are compiled.
